newsitem.title: UK: Genetic screening for life insurance seen overdone.
newsitem.headline: Genetic screening for life insurance seen overdone.

text.p: Fears that genetic screening could undermine the life insurance industry are exaggerated, Healthcare International said in a report from the Economist Intelligence Unit on Thursday.
But "when it comes to health insurance, concerns could be more relevant," the EIU said in a statement.
Concerns have been growing for some time that advances in genetic testing for a growing number of diseases could lead to discrimination in access to life and health insurance.

The report said the predictive quality of gene testing for life insurers will be limited because the genetic make-up of most common killer diseases is so complex that testing will provide little additional information.

But for health care costs and health insurance, the report said "ethicists fear that insurers will 'cherry pick,' covering only people who are unlikely to fall ill. For individuals prone to disease, premiums could become unaffordable."

The sensible method of pooling risk is universal participation in healthcare, but "the resolution to drive through such reform would not appear until the middle classes find it difficult to obtain affordable coverage," the report said.
Alastair Kent, director of the Genetic Interest Group (GIG) agreed that access to insurance for health and long-term care were far more likely to be affected than simple life policies.

"The crucial issue is the extent to which commercial organisations are able to demonstrate their competency to interpret genetic information," he told Reuters. GIG campaigns on behalf of people with genetic disorders.
Insurers in the UK and Germany have opted for self-regulation in the field of genetic testing, but Belgium, Austria and Norway have banned insurers from using DNA test results, the report said.
France has a five-year moratorium. The Netherlands is temporarily allowing testing as part of medical underwriting on some life policies.
In the U.S., there are no controls over life insurers using genetic screening, but 13 states have passed laws barring its use to calculate premiums for health insurance, the report added.
